newsitem.title: INDIA: India wheat output seen rising after dip last year.
newsitem.headline: India wheat output seen rising after dip last year.

text.p: India expects a good wheat crop this year after a dip in output last year that forced imports, government officials said on Wednesday.
"The production prospects are fairly good," said M.S. Bhatia, adviser in the Agriculture Ministry.
"We are expecting anywhere in the range of 64-65 million tonnes, two million tonnes more than last year," Bhatia told Reuters.
India set a target of 66 million tonnes of wheat for the 1996/97 (July/June) crop year.
India's wheat output fell to 62.6 million tonnes in the 1995/96 crop year from 65.47 million tonnes in 1994/95.
Officials said rust disease in the northern state of Punjab and high temperatures during harvesting time in March 1996 had contributed to low output in 1995/96.
Punjab contributes around 20 percent to the country's wheat production.
In December, India decided to import two million tonnes of wheat in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.
India last imported wheat in 1992/93, buying two million tonnes. It exported 600,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and 1.07 million tonnes between April and September 1996 when the government halted exports.
Government wheat procurement in the 1995/96 growing season fell to 8.2 million tonnes from 12.3 million tonnes a year earlier due to a three-million-tonne shortfall in output.
Officials said as of January 1, 1997, the government had wheat stocks of 6.7 million tonnes, about one million tonnes less than the buffer stock requirement on that date.

Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav said in January that in view of the depleted wheat stocks the government might have to examine various options including bringing forward the procurement season by a fortnight to March 16.
India's wheat crop is due for harvest in March after a ninth consecutive good monsoon.
"We have to wait for two or three weeks to get a clear picture. We have to be careful about winter rains," said E.A. Sidiq of the Indian Council of Agriculture Research.
Sidiq said this year winter had set in early in India's northern region and the temperature in the next few days would be a crucial factor.
"If the temperature shoots up in late February or early March it is not good for wheat. Temperature is a deciding factor," Sidiq told Reuters.
He said the crop prospects were good and the country should achieve the production target of 66 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Officials of the government-run State Trading Corporation said they had so far contracted for imports of 1.48 million tonnes of wheat in fiscal 1996/97 (April/March).
"About 160,000 tonnes of wheat had arrived in January. We expect another 500,000 tonnes to arrive during February," said one STC official.
Bhatia said it was too early to talk in terms of India getting back to the wheat export market. "I don't think we should go for exports of wheat at this stage."
